title: The merchant and the parrot
hookLine: a caged parrot asks its merchant to greet the wild parrots of India (Masnavi 1.1547ff)

lines: SAY HI TO EVERYONE FOR ME.
cards: Somebody you love is going somewhere you can't. A cousin flying back to the country your family came from. A friend going home to the town you both grew up in.
You say, without thinking: say hi to everyone for me. Tell them I miss them. It's a small line that says: part of me belongs there.

Rumi's next story starts with that exact request. A rich merchant is getting ready for a long trip to India, and before he goes, he makes the rounds of his household. Today, the merchant and the parrot.

teach.h: WHAT SHALL I BRING YOU FROM INDIA?
teach.b: The merchant is generous. He asks every servant and every member of the household: what shall I bring you from India? Each one names something.
Then he comes to his parrot, a beautiful, clever bird in a cage. What gift do you want?

teach.h: THE PARROT ASKS FOR A MESSAGE.
teach.b: The parrot asks for no gift at all, only a message. When you see the parrots of India flying free in the forests, it says, give them my greeting.
Tell them a parrot who longs for them is shut in a cage in my house, by the turning of fate. Ask them: is it right that I waste away here while you fly among the trees? Is this what friends do?
Remember me when you're in the meadows at dawn. That's the whole request: greet them for me. Rumi pauses here for long reflections.

teach.h: IS IT RIGHT I'M CAGED, YOU FREE?
teach.b: Sufi readers take the caged parrot as the human soul, kept in the cage of the body and this world, and the wild parrots as the saints, the friends of God, who are already free.

teach.h: THE SOUL, AND THE FREE FRIENDS.
teach.b: The message is the soul's longing, sent home. You can hear the reed from earlier in this camp: cut from the reedbed, and crying for it. Look back at the week.
In Rumi's story, the lion argued for tying the camel, a hare walked slowly on purpose, and the lion drowned fighting his own face, while Rumi pointed to the lion inside.
In Marcus's notebook, cracked bread had its own beauty, and a person could stand upright, not propped. Two books, kept apart, and the week ends with a small caged bird asking only to be remembered.
Tomorrow, the message arrives in India, and something happens nobody expected.

how: The merchant and the parrot is a story from the Masnavi's first book; Sufi teachers read the caged parrot as the soul and the parrots of India as the free friends of God.

a Persian travel diary of journeys to India
Rumi's long work of stories and reflections

games.q: you're a caged parrot. your master is going to the land where your kind fly free, and asks what gift you want. what do you ask for?
o: a message carried to the free parrots.
games.why: the parrot asks only for its greeting to be carried: is it right that I'm caged while you fly free?

practice: Let someone come to mind who's far away: across the country, across an ocean, or across a silence that's grown too long. What would you want them to hear?
Not news, just: I remember you, I miss you, I'm still here; hold those words for a minute.

wordCard.voice: Masnavi, Rumi's book of stories: a caged parrot asks for no gift, only that its master greet the free parrots of India for it. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian: parrot. in Sufi poetry, often the soul that can speak.

carryVoice: Your line: greet them for me. No gift, just a greeting. And that's the week.
